sections.title: Vectors Basics and Unit Vectors
sections.content: A vector has both magnitude and direction. A unit vector 'a^' has a magnitude of 1 and gives the direction of vector 'a'. Formula: a^ = a / |a|. The position vector of a point (x, y, z) is xi + yj + zk.

sections.title: Dot Product (Scalar Product)
sections.content: The dot product of a and b is a.b = |a||b|cos(theta), where theta is the angle between them. If a and b are perpendicular, a.b = 0. Also, i.i = j.j = k.k = 1, and i.j = j.k = k.i = 0.

sections.title: Cross Product (Vector Product)
sections.content: The cross product of a and b is a x b = |a||b|sin(theta) n^, where n^ is a unit vector perpendicular to both a and b (Right-Hand Rule). If a and b are parallel, a x b = 0. Note: a x b = -(b x a).

sections.title: Direction Cosines and Direction Ratios (3D)
sections.content: Direction Cosines (l, m, n) are the cosines of angles (alpha, beta, gamma) a line makes with x, y, and z axes. l = cos(alpha), m = cos(beta), n = cos(gamma). Direction Ratios (a, b, c) are any numbers proportional to l, m, n.

sections.title: Equation of a Line in 3D (Basic)
sections.content: Vector form: r = a + t*b, where 'a' is a point on the line and 'b' is a parallel vector. Cartesian form: (x-x1)/a = (y-y1)/b = (z-z1)/c, where (x1,y1,z1) is the point and (a,b,c) are direction ratios.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
1) Confusing dot product (yields a scalar/number) with cross product (yields a vector).
2) Assuming l + m + n = 1 (The correct relation is l^2 + m^2 + n^2 = 1).
3) Forgetting to check if DRs given in a line equation are actually divided by 1, e.g., (2x-1)/3 must be written as (x - 1/2)/(3/2).

sections.title: Quick Summary
sections.content: Level 1 establishes vector algebra (dot and cross products) and translates 2D coordinate geometry into 3D using Direction Ratios/Cosines and the basic equation of a straight line.

tricks.title: Projection of a Vector
tricks.explanation: The projection of vector 'a' on vector 'b' is given by (a.b) / |b|. Think of it as 'dot product divided by the magnitude of the base vector'.
tricks.example: Projection of 2i+j on i+j is [(2)(1) + (1)(1)] / sqrt(2) = 3/sqrt(2).

tricks.title: Area of Parallelogram & Triangle
tricks.explanation: If a and b are adjacent sides, Area of Parallelogram = |a x b|. Area of Triangle = 1/2 |a x b|. If diagonals d1 and d2 are given, Area of Parallelogram = 1/2 |d1 x d2|.
tricks.example: For sides i and j, Area = |i x j| = |k| = 1.

tricks.title: Parallel Vectors Check (Collinearity)
tricks.explanation: If vector a = a1i + a2j + a3k and b = b1i + b2j + b3k are parallel, their components are proportional: a1/b1 = a2/b2 = a3/b3 = lambda.

tricks.title: Direction Cosines Property
tricks.explanation: The sum of the squares of Direction Cosines is always 1: l^2 + m^2 + n^2 = 1. Consequently, sin^2(alpha) + sin^2(beta) + sin^2(gamma) = 2.
tricks.example: If a line makes 45 and 60 degrees with x and y axes, cos^2(45) + cos^2(60) + n^2 = 1 -> 1/2 + 1/4 + n^2 = 1 -> n = +-1/2 (60 or 120 degrees).

tricks.title: Angle Between Two Vectors
tricks.explanation: Use the dot product to quickly find the angle: cos(theta) = (a.b) / (|a||b|). If a.b > 0, angle is acute. If a.b < 0, angle is obtuse.
tricks.example: a=i, b=j. a.b = 0 -> cos(theta) = 0 -> theta = 90 degrees.

tricks.title: Centroid of a 3D Triangle
tricks.explanation: Just like in 2D, the centroid G of a triangle with vertices A(x1,y1,z1), B(x2,y2,z2), C(x3,y3,z3) is ((x1+x2+x3)/3, (y1+y2+y3)/3, (z1+z2+z3)/3).
